decks.domain: Backing up, traffic signals and signs

cards.front: What should you do before getting in to back up, and why?
cards.back: Before you get in to back up, look behind the vehicle, because small children and small objects cannot be seen from the driver seat.

cards.front: How should your hands, arm and eyes be positioned when reversing?
cards.back: To reverse, keep a foot on the brake while shifting, grip the top of the wheel, the twelve o'clock spot, with your left hand, rest your right arm on the passenger seat back and look over your shoulder out the rear window.

cards.front: How should a rear-view camera be used when backing up?
cards.back: Mirrors do not show the space right behind the car, so a rear-view camera, if you have one, is used together with mirrors and an over-the-shoulder look, never instead of them.

cards.front: How should you back up, and where do you look while turning in reverse?
cards.back: Back up slowly and smoothly, steering a little toward where the rear should go; when turning in reverse, glance quickly to the front and sides and keep looking back until fully stopped.

decks.domain: Backing up, traffic signals and signs

cards.front: Besides signals, signs and markings, who can direct traffic, and must you follow them?
cards.back: Traffic is controlled by signals, signs and pavement markings, and also by police, highway workers and school crossing guards, whose directions you are required to follow.

cards.front: How are signal lights usually arranged?
cards.back: Signal lights are normally arranged with red at the top, yellow in the middle and green at the bottom, though some places use a single red, yellow or green light.

cards.front: What should you do at an intersection where the signal is dark or broken?
cards.back: If a traffic signal is dark or not working properly, handle the intersection as a four-way stop.

cards.front: Does a broken signal give the busier road the right to go?
cards.back: A dark or broken signal is handled as a four-way stop, not as a green light for the busier road.

decks.domain: Backing up, traffic signals and signs

cards.front: What does a steady red light require, and when may you turn right on red?
cards.back: At a steady red light, stop and wait for green; after stopping and yielding to pedestrians and traffic, a right turn on red is allowed unless a sign forbids it.

cards.front: When is a left turn on red legal?
cards.back: Turning left on red is legal only when both streets are one-way, going from one onto the other, after you stop and yield, and only if no sign prohibits it.

cards.front: How does a right turn on red differ from a left turn on red?
cards.back: Right on red is allowed at most intersections after a full stop, but left on red works only when turning from one one-way street into a second one.

cards.front: What does a steady yellow light mean?
cards.back: A steady yellow light warns that red is coming next, so stop unless you are already inside the intersection.

cards.front: What may you do on a steady green, and whom must you yield to first?
cards.back: On a steady green you may go straight or turn either way unless a sign bans the turn, but first yield to any vehicle or pedestrian already in the intersection or the crosswalk next to it.

decks.domain: Backing up, traffic signals and signs

cards.front: What does a lit red arrow mean?
cards.back: A lit red arrow means stop, and you may not turn in the direction it points.

cards.front: What does a green arrow allow, and what if it goes dark while the round green stays on?
cards.back: A green arrow, shown alone or with another light, lets you turn the way it points; if the arrow goes dark while the round green stays on, you may still turn after yielding to through traffic and pedestrians unless a sign or red arrow forbids it.

cards.front: When the green arrow goes out but the round green stays on, may you still turn?
cards.back: If the green arrow goes out but the round green remains, the turn is still allowed, now only after yielding; a red arrow means no turn that way at all.

cards.front: What does a steady yellow arrow warn of?
cards.back: A steady yellow arrow warns that a red arrow is about to appear, so stop unless you are already in the intersection.

cards.front: What does a flashing yellow arrow allow, and what follows it?
cards.back: A flashing yellow arrow lets a left-turning driver go carefully only after yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians; it then turns solid yellow, meaning do not enter if you can stop safely, and finally red, meaning stop.

decks.domain: Backing up, traffic signals and signs

cards.front: How do you treat a flashing red light?
cards.back: Treat a flashing red light exactly like a stop sign: come to a stop, then move on once pedestrians and other traffic have been given the right of way.

cards.front: How does a steady red light differ from a flashing red light?
cards.back: Steady red means stop and wait for green, while flashing red means stop and then proceed when clear, just as at a stop sign.

cards.front: What does a flashing yellow light mean?
cards.back: A flashing yellow light warns of a hazard ahead, so slow down and continue with caution.

cards.front: How does a flashing yellow light differ from a flashing yellow arrow?
cards.back: Flashing yellow light and flashing yellow arrow differ: the plain flashing light warns of a hazard, while the flashing arrow permits a left turn only after yielding to oncoming traffic and walkers.

cards.front: What is a HAWK signal for?
cards.back: A HAWK signal, short for High Intensity Activated Crosswalk, helps pedestrians cross by flashing a yellow and red sequence that tells drivers someone needs to cross.

decks.domain: Backing up, traffic signals and signs

cards.front: What kinds of information do road signs give, and what do shape and color tell you?
cards.back: Signs tell you rules, hazards, where you are, directions and nearby services, and a sign's shape and color show what kind of message it carries.

cards.front: What do regulatory signs do, and what colors do they use?
cards.back: Regulatory signs state the law at a location, use black or red on a white background, and disobeying one is a traffic violation.

cards.front: What do speed limit signs tell you, and when must you go slower?
cards.back: Speed limit signs give the highest or lowest speed allowed; the highest limit assumes ideal conditions, so you must slow down when conditions demand it.

cards.front: Where must you stop at a stop sign?
cards.back: At a stop sign, stop completely at the marked stop line; with no line, stop before the near-side crosswalk; with neither, stop at the point closest to the cross road where you can see approaching traffic.

cards.front: In what order do you choose your stopping point at a stop sign?
cards.back: The stopping point at a stop sign follows an order: the stop line first, then the near-side crosswalk, then the spot nearest the cross road with a view of traffic.

cards.front: What does a yield sign require?
cards.back: A yield sign means slow down, or stop if needed, to let every pedestrian and any vehicle that has the right of way go first.

decks.domain: Backing up, traffic signals and signs

cards.front: What do Do Not Enter and Wrong Way signs tell a driver?
cards.back: Do Not Enter and Wrong Way signs warn and turn back drivers heading the wrong way on a street or freeway ramp; never drive past one.

cards.front: What does a One Way sign mean?
cards.back: A One Way sign means you may travel only in the direction its arrow points.

cards.front: How does a One Way sign differ from a Wrong Way sign?
cards.back: A One Way sign tells you which single direction a street allows, while Do Not Enter and Wrong Way signs tell a driver already facing the wrong direction to go no further.
cards.memory_hook: one way guides, wrong way stops

cards.front: What do lane control signs show?
cards.back: Lane control signs, placed beside or above the road and often using arrows, show where you may turn; similar arrows are sometimes painted on the pavement.

cards.front: What do prohibited signs show?
cards.back: Prohibited signs show an action you may not take, such as making a U-turn or a left turn.

decks.module: Warning, rail, work and guide signs
decks.domain: Backing up, traffic signals and signs

cards.front: What colors are warning signs, and what do they alert you to?
cards.back: Warning signs are yellow or fluorescent green with black symbols and alert you to things like school zones, curves, slippery pavement, merging traffic or busy pedestrian areas; a merge sign, for example, warns of cars joining from a side street.

cards.front: What do advisory speed signs give?
cards.back: Advisory speed signs are cautionary signs giving the safe speed for curves, corners and off-ramps under ideal conditions.

cards.front: What are the key safety rules at a railroad crossing?
cards.back: Railroad crossing signs come in several shapes; never race a train, never start across until there is room for your whole vehicle beyond the far side, and do not shift gears on the tracks in case the engine stalls.

cards.front: What do the blue railroad emergency notification signs provide?
cards.back: Blue railroad emergency notification system signs at every highway-rail grade crossing list a phone number for reporting problems, and the Department of Transportation number printed below it identifies that exact crossing.

cards.front: What color are work zone signs, and what are they for?
cards.back: Work zone signs are orange with black letters or symbols and are used with other devices or flaggers to steer traffic through work areas and protect road workers.

cards.front: What do guide signs look like, and what do they give?
cards.back: Guide signs have a green background and give directions and mileage to particular destinations.

cards.front: What do blue signs and brown signs point you to?
cards.back: Blue signs direct you to service facilities, while brown signs mark recreational, historic or cultural areas.

cards.front: Which sign colors go with warning, work zone, guide, service and recreation signs?
cards.back: Warning signs are yellow or fluorescent green, work zone signs are orange, guide signs are green, service signs are blue and recreation signs are brown.

recap_hooks.text: Look behind before getting in, look over your shoulder while reversing, and use a camera only with mirrors and a look back.
Follow officers, workers and crossing guards, and treat a dark signal as a four-way stop.
Right on red is allowed after a full stop unless a sign forbids it; left on red only from one one-way street onto another.
Steady yellow warns of red, and green still means yield first.
A red arrow means no turn that way; if a green arrow goes out but round green stays, turn after yielding.
A flashing yellow arrow allows a left turn only after yielding.
Flashing red is a stop sign, flashing yellow means caution, and a HAWK signal means a pedestrian needs to cross.
Regulatory signs state the law; stop at the line, then the crosswalk, then where you can see traffic.
One Way means follow the arrow; Do Not Enter and Wrong Way mean turn back.

recaps.module: Warning, rail, work and guide signs

recap_hooks.text: Warning signs are yellow, work zones orange, guide signs green, services blue and recreation brown.
Never race a train, and cross only when your whole vehicle fits beyond the tracks.
